yaml.description: Short explanations of recurring terms used across The Curious Notebook.

markdown.markdown:
This glossary collects short explanations of terms that appear across the notebook.

The goal is not to replace textbooks or review papers. The goal is to make the notes easier to read without having to define 
every term from scratch each time.


Reservoir computing is a machine learning approach where an input is passed through a fixed dynamical system called a reservoir. 
The reservoir transforms the input into a richer set of states. A simple readout is then trained to produce the desired output.

The reservoir itself is usually not trained.

## Physical reservoir computing

Physical reservoir computing uses a physical system as the reservoir.

Instead of simulating all transformations in software, the input is applied to a real or simulated physical system. 
The system’s response becomes the reservoir state.

Examples could include soft bodies, mechanical networks, fluids, optical systems, electronic circuits, or magnetic materials.

## Dynamical system

A dynamical system is a system whose state changes over time according to some rule.

The state could describe position, velocity, voltage, pressure, temperature, neural activity, or many other quantities. 
In this notebook, dynamical systems are usually interesting because their current state depends on both the current input and the 
recent past.

## State

The state of a system is the set of variables used to describe what the system is doing at a given time.

For a mechanical oscillator, the state might include position and velocity. For a neural reservoir, it might include neuron 
voltages or spike counts. For a soft body, it might include deformation at different points.

## Readout

A readout is the trained part of a reservoir computer.

The reservoir transforms the input, and the readout learns how to map the reservoir states to the desired output. In many reservoir 
computing systems, the readout is a simple linear model.

## Memory

Memory describes how much information about past inputs is still present in the current state of the system.

A reservoir with useful memory does not only respond to the present input. It also carries traces of what happened recently.

## Nonlinearity

A nonlinear system is one where the output is not simply proportional to the input.

Nonlinearity is important because it can create richer transformations of the input. In reservoir computing, useful computation often comes from a combination of memory and nonlinearity.

## Coupling

Coupling describes how different parts of a system influence each other.

In a network of oscillators, coupling determines how motion in one oscillator affects the others. In a soft body, coupling may come from material deformation. In a neural system, coupling may come from synaptic connections.

## Oscillator

An oscillator is a system that tends to repeat its motion over time.

Examples include pendulums, springs, vibrating beams, electrical circuits, and biological rhythms. Oscillators are useful toy systems because their dynamics can show memory, resonance, synchronization, and phase relationships.

## Transient response

A transient response is the temporary behavior of a system after an input or disturbance.

In reservoir computing, transient responses are often useful because they contain information about how the system reacted to recent inputs.

## High-dimensional representation

A high-dimensional representation describes an input using many variables instead of just one or two.

Reservoirs are useful partly because they can turn a simple input signal into many internal states. This gives the readout more features to work with.

## Embodiment

Embodiment refers to the idea that a physical body can participate in sensing, control, or computation.

In robotics, this means the body is not just something to be controlled. Its material properties and dynamics can help shape behavior.
